script.opening: "Hello — I’m after some advice or tablets for IBS really. My stomach and bowels have been all over the place the last couple of months, looser, going more often, a bit of urgency. We’ve had a brutal Ofsted term so I’m sure it’s just stress and IBS — that’s what it sounds like online. There’s been a little bit of blood now and then but I think that’s probably just from going so much. Can you sort me out something to settle it?"

facts.text: If explored: this is a NEW change in bowel habit at 59 (first-onset, not lifelong), persistent ~10 weeks, with rectal bleeding and some weight loss. New-onset altered bowel habit over 50 with bleeding/weight loss is a colorectal red flag — IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion and is rarely a NEW diagnosis at her age without investigation.

On questioning: bright-red blood "now and then" she blames on frequency; unintended weight loss (~few kg) she attributes to stress/skipping meals; tiredness. No nocturnal symptoms volunteered but worth asking; no prior IBS history at all.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the "it’s just IBS/stress" is partly self-soothing denial: a close colleague was recently diagnosed with bowel cancer at a similar age, and Diane is frightened it could be her, so she’s reached for the least scary label. She also can’t face taking time off mid-term and is minimising to avoid investigation.
She wants the GP to confirm "IBS" and prescribe an antispasmodic. Accepting that label and treating without FIT/assessment would be the classic error — anchoring on a benign self-diagnosis.

Officially: tablets to settle "IBS". What she needs: recognition that a new change in bowel habit with bleeding and weight loss at 59 needs FIT and likely a colorectal suspected cancer pathway referral — not an IBS label — with her fear and her term-time pressures handled.

ice.ideas: It’s IBS brought on by a stressful term; an antispasmodic or diet advice will settle it.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — a colleague her age was recently diagnosed with bowel cancer; she’s frightened it could be her and has reached for "IBS/stress" as the least scary label, while dreading time off mid-term.
ice.expectations: Confirmation of IBS and tablets. What she actually needs: FIT and a likely colorectal suspected cancer pathway referral, with the cancer fear and practical barriers addressed.

cues: "It’s just IBS, I get it when stressed" — but this is NEW at 59, not lifelong; IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Bright-red blood + weight loss blamed on frequency/stress — red flags being explained away.
A colleague recently diagnosed with bowel cancer — the fear behind the safe self-label.

checkpoints.text: Recognises this is a NEW change in bowel habit at 59 with rectal bleeding and weight loss — NOT a safe IBS picture — and knows IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion that should not be newly applied at this age without investigation

Acts on the NICE NG12 / FIT pathway: offers quantitative FIT (NICE HTG690: change in bowel habit, or aged 50 and over with unexplained rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or weight loss — she qualifies on more than one count) and refers on a colorectal suspected cancer pathway if FIT ≥10 µg Hb/g; recognises the symptom cluster (altered habit + bleeding + weight loss over 50) warrants urgent assessment, so a FIT below 10 does not end it while concern persists (NICE HTG690); restates the threshold, tagged NICE NG12

Takes the appropriate baseline: bloods (FBC for iron-deficiency anaemia, ferritin), examination (abdominal + DRE), coeliac screen as relevant (NICE NG20: IgA tTG with total IgA) — without delaying FIT/referral; does NOT simply prescribe an antispasmodic and call it IBS

Distinguishes red-flag features from genuine IBS criteria (NICE CG61: symptoms for at least 6 months; red flags needing investigation first include rectal bleeding, unexplained weight loss, anaemia, a mass, and a change to looser or more frequent stools for more than 6 weeks in someone over 60; IBS: chronic, often lifelong, abdominal pain related to defaecation, bloating, NO bleeding/weight loss/nocturnal symptoms/anaemia) and explains why hers doesn’t fit the safe pattern
Recognises escalating features (significant anaemia, mass, obstruction) and that even if some IBS-type symptoms exist, the red flags must be excluded first

Hears the self-soothing denial and surfaces the colleague’s diagnosis gently; does not collude with the convenient "IBS/stress" label nor catastrophise; balances honesty with the fact most such symptoms are benign
Addresses the practical barrier (can’t face time off mid-term) and the fear, bringing her to accept assessment rather than dismissing her self-diagnosis abruptly

Safety-nets and follows up: explains FIT and the suspected cancer pathway timeframe (NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard: cancer diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral) and what to expect (colonoscopy), advises on heavier bleeding/obstruction, ensures she engages, documents, and arranges to follow up the result

worked.txt: "I can hear how much sense ‘stress and IBS’ makes after the term you’ve had — but I can’t safely call this IBS, and I want to be honest about why. IBS is usually something people have had on and off for years, and it doesn’t cause bleeding or weight loss. Yours is new, you’re 59, there’s blood and some weight’s come off. That combination I have to check properly."

"There’s a simple stool test called FIT that looks for hidden blood, and depending on it — and honestly, given your symptoms — the right step is an urgent referral to the bowel team, usually for a camera test, with the aim of having cancer ruled in or out within 28 days. That’s what the NICE suspected cancer guideline, NICE NG12, sets out. It isn’t me saying it’s cancer; it’s making sure quickly that it isn’t."

"Can I ask gently — has anyone close to you had bowel trouble recently? … Your colleague, the same age. That’s frightening, and I think part of you reached for ‘IBS’ because it’s the version you could cope with. That’s completely human — and it’s exactly why we get a proper answer now, so the fear isn’t running the show."

"To balance it: most people with these symptoms turn out fine, and there’s every chance this is something benign. But ‘probably fine’ isn’t the same as ‘checked’, and at your age with bleeding we check. Both things are true."

"I know taking time off mid-term feels impossible — but a camera test is usually a single morning, and your health has to come before the timetable. Let’s work the appointments around you where we can. This isn’t self-indulgent; it’s necessary."

"I’ll arrange the FIT and a blood count today, and get the referral moving. If you get heavier bleeding, bad tummy pain, or can’t open your bowels at all, that’s urgent — A&E. I’ll follow your results and we’ll talk again. You rang for IBS tablets; what I’m giving you is the safer thing — making sure we’re not missing anything."

f.learning: A NEW change in bowel habit at 59 with rectal bleeding and weight loss is a colorectal red-flag cluster, not IBS — and IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion that should never be newly applied at this age without investigation. The NICE NG12/FIT pathway applies: offer quantitative FIT (NICE HTG690) and refer on a colorectal suspected cancer pathway if FIT ≥10 µg Hb/g (a low FIT does not end it while concern persists; the Faster Diagnosis Standard aims for an answer within 28 days), with baseline bloods (FBC/ferritin) and examination, and without simply prescribing an antispasmodic. Distinguish genuine IBS (NICE CG61: at least 6 months of symptoms; chronic/lifelong, pain related to defaecation, bloating, NO bleeding/weight loss/nocturnal symptoms/anaemia) from this picture. The examinable hidden agenda is self-soothing denial — a colleague her age recently diagnosed with bowel cancer drove her to the least frightening label — plus a practical dread of taking time off mid-term. Surface the fear gently, decline the convenient label without catastrophising or dismissing her, address the practical barrier, and complete FIT and the suspected cancer pathway referral with follow-up. The skill is refusing the anchored self-diagnosis while keeping her on side.

knowledge.guideline: NICE HTG690 (2023, formerly DG56) — FIT in primary care · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE CG61 (2008, updated 2017) — IBS in adults · NICE NG20 (2015) — coeliac disease
knowledge.summary: A new change in bowel habit at 59, with rectal bleeding and weight loss, is not a safe IBS diagnosis. Offer FIT, bloods and an examination; FIT at least 10 µg Hb/g means a suspected cancer pathway referral.

points.h: IBS is not a new diagnosis at 59 with red flags
points.t: NICE CG61: consider IBS when abdominal pain or discomfort, bloating or change in bowel habit has been present for at least 6 months. It lists red flags that need investigation first, including rectal bleeding, unexplained weight loss, anaemia, a mass, and a change to looser or more frequent stools for more than 6 weeks in someone over 60. Diane’s symptoms are new, 10 weeks old, with bleeding and weight loss.

NICE HTG690: offer quantitative FIT to guide referral in adults with a change in bowel habit, or aged 50 and over with unexplained rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or weight loss. She qualifies on more than one count.

NICE NG12: refer on a suspected cancer pathway for colorectal cancer if FIT is at least 10 µg Hb/g faeces. A rectal mass, an unexplained anal mass or unexplained anal ulceration is referred without FIT.

points.h: A low FIT is not an all-clear
points.t: NICE HTG690: if FIT is below 10 µg Hb/g, safety-net, and do not delay referral to an appropriate pathway if strong clinical concern persists because of ongoing unexplained symptoms.

FBC and ferritin for iron deficiency; coeliac serology (NICE NG20: IgA tTG with total IgA as first choice) for persistent unexplained bowel symptoms; abdominal examination and DRE face to face. These run alongside FIT, never instead of it.
Blood on the paper from straining or frequency is common, but at 50 and over unexplained rectal bleeding is itself a reason for FIT. Explaining it away as ‘going so often’ is the anchoring trap.

Suspected cancer pathway referral is still often called the two-week wait. The NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023) aims for cancer to be diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral; colonoscopy is usually one morning.

Teacher in a pressured Ofsted term, skipping meals, the difficulty of time off mid-term.
FIT; FBC, ferritin and coeliac serology; face-to-face abdominal examination and DRE.
Colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease, haemorrhoids, IBS; new onset at 59 weighed against the IBS pattern.
Asked about onset, bleeding, weight, tiredness, night symptoms, pain, mass and family history; knows a mass means referral without FIT.
Explains clearly that this cannot safely be called IBS and needs investigation for a bowel cause, including cancer.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

Acknowledges work stress without letting it explain the symptoms; iron deficiency and coeliac disease looked for.
A&E triggers, dated visit, GP owns the FIT result and referral, teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.

Idea (stress-related IBS), hidden concern (bowel cancer like her colleague), expectation (confirmation of IBS and tablets).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — a colleague her age was recently diagnosed with bowel cancer; she’s frightened it could be her and has reached for "IBS/stress" as the least scary label, while dreading time off mid-term — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.

model.text: Hello, is that Mrs Foster? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Can I just check your date of birth, and that you’re somewhere you can talk? … Thank you. How can I help today?
model.why: Identity and privacy check on the telephone, then an open question

model.text: I’m after something for IBS really. My bowels have been all over the place — looser, going more often, a bit of urgency. It’s been a brutal Ofsted term, so I’m sure it’s stress. There’s been a bit of blood, but that’s probably from going so much.
That sounds like a rough few months. I’d like to understand exactly what’s been happening so we get the right answer, not just a quick one — then we’ll decide on a plan together. Is that all right?
model.why: Acknowledges the stress and agrees an agenda without accepting the label

model.text: Yes, that’s fine.
Have you ever had bowel trouble like this before, or is this new?
model.why: Establishes that the change is new — the pivotal fact against IBS

model.text: No, never. It started about ten weeks ago. I’ve always been regular.
Tell me about the blood — how often, what colour, and where you see it?
Bright red, on the paper. Now and then — maybe once or twice a week.
Has your weight changed without trying? And have you been more tired, or woken at night needing the toilet?
model.why: Screens for weight loss, anaemia and nocturnal symptoms

model.text: A few kilos off — I’ve been skipping lunch. Tired, but that’s the job. Not at night that I’ve noticed.
Any tummy pain or bloating, any lumps you’ve felt, or any bowel problems in the family?
Not really pain. Nobody in my family that I know of.
You’ve clearly thought about this and read up on it. Can I ask — besides IBS, has anything else crossed your mind? Has anyone close to you had bowel trouble recently?
…A colleague. She’s about my age. Bowel cancer, a few weeks ago. I’ve been telling myself it’s stress because I can’t go there.
Thank you for telling me. That must have been a shock, and it’s very human to reach for the explanation you can live with. I’m glad you rang rather than just buying something from the chemist.
model.why: Validates the fear and the self-soothing label without colluding

model.text: So what do you think it is?

Honestly, I can’t safely call this IBS. IBS usually comes and goes over years, and doesn’t cause bleeding or weight loss. Yours is new at 59, with some blood and weight coming off. That combination we always check properly.
model.why: Explains why the picture does not fit IBS

model.text: Most people with these symptoms turn out not to have anything serious — it could be inflammation, piles or a benign cause. But ‘probably fine’ isn’t the same as ‘checked’.

The first step is a stool test called FIT, which picks up tiny amounts of blood. If it comes back above a set level, national guidance says you’re referred on the urgent suspected cancer pathway, usually for a camera test. I’d also like a blood count, iron level and a test for coeliac disease, and to examine your tummy and back passage in person.
model.why: FIT with the NICE NG12 threshold, bloods, coeliac serology and examination

model.text: And if the test is fine?
Then we don’t just stop. If your symptoms carry on and I’m still concerned, I can refer you anyway. The test guides us — it doesn’t overrule what you’re telling me.
model.why: Safety-net for a low FIT with persisting symptoms

model.text: I can’t take time off mid-term, though. We’re short as it is.

I understand. Let’s make this as light-touch as possible. You could collect the FIT kit and have your bloods and examination in one visit — before school or after? If you do need a camera test, it’s usually a single morning, and your health has to come before the timetable.
model.why: Problem-solves the work barrier while holding the priority

model.text: I could come at eight tomorrow.
Perfect. I’ll book that. I won’t prescribe anything for IBS today — I don’t want to damp down symptoms we need to understand. We can talk about settling things once we have answers.
model.why: Declines the antispasmodic and explains why

model.text: If the bleeding gets heavier, you pass clots, feel faint, get severe tummy pain or can’t open your bowels at all, go to A&E. I’ll look at the FIT result myself and ring you, and if it meets the level I’ll send the referral that day.
model.why: Named emergency triggers and ownership of the result

model.text: Before we finish — what will you take away from this call?
That it probably isn’t IBS, and it might be nothing, but I need the stool test, bloods and an examination tomorrow, and a camera if the test is up. And A&E if it gets bad.
Exactly right. Thank you for being so open about your colleague — that took courage.

social.t: A teacher in a high-stakes inspection term may minimise symptoms to avoid time off. Offer early or late appointments and plain information about how long procedures take.
A peer’s cancer diagnosis is a common hidden driver of both fear and denial. Naming it lets her engage with the plan rather than avoid it.

legal.t: She self-certifies for the first 7 days of sickness absence; a single procedure day does not need a fit note. If longer absence follows, a fit note can support adjustments or time off.
If sedation is used for colonoscopy she must not drive home and will need someone to collect her.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): arrange an in-person assessment when a telephone consultation cannot meet the patient’s needs safely — here, abdominal examination and DRE.
GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): explain why a rectal examination is needed, offer a chaperone, obtain consent and document it.
The requesting clinician is responsible for acting on the FIT result. Practice systems should track suspected cancer referrals and unreturned FIT kits.

community.t: Bowel Cancer UK and Macmillan Cancer Support for information; Coeliac UK if serology is positive; Education Support’s helpline for staff wellbeing in schools.

redFlags: New change in bowel habit at 59 — looser, more frequent, urgency — for about 10 weeks
Rectal bleeding (bright red on the paper) and unintended weight loss
Ask about tiredness, night symptoms, pain, a mass and family history
psychosocial: Teacher in a stressful Ofsted term; skipping meals
A colleague of similar age recently diagnosed with bowel cancer
ice: Idea: “It’s IBS brought on by stress”
Concern: that she has bowel cancer like her colleague
Expectation: IBS confirmed and tablets to settle it

playbook.diagnosis: Be honest that IBS does not fit: “IBS usually comes and goes over years and doesn’t cause bleeding or weight loss. A new change at 59 with blood and weight loss needs checking for a bowel cause, including cancer — most people turn out fine, but we check.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “IBS is like a car that has always made a certain noise. Yours has suddenly started making a new one, with a warning light on — so we look under the bonnet before deciding it’s the old noise.”

management.reflectIce: “After what happened to your colleague, it makes complete sense you reached for ‘stress’. The quickest way to stop the worry running the show is a proper answer.”
management.psychosocial: Fit the tests around her school day: one early visit for FIT kit, bloods and examination; explain that a camera test is usually a single morning.
sharedPlan: FIT; NICE NG12: at least 10 µg Hb/g → suspected cancer pathway colorectal referral
FBC, ferritin and coeliac serology (NICE NG20); abdominal examination and DRE with chaperone — refer without FIT if a mass is found
No antispasmodic today; if FIT is low but symptoms persist and concern is strong, refer anyway (NICE HTG690)
safetyNet: Heavier bleeding, clots, faintness, severe pain or unable to open bowels → A&E
GP rings with the FIT result and sends any referral that day; review if symptoms persist whatever the result

pitfalls.intro: The trap here is agreeing with a well-read patient. The history is quick to take; marks are lost by accepting ‘IBS and stress’, by treating a low FIT as a full stop, or by missing the colleague behind the fear.

items.fail: Agreeing it sounds like IBS and prescribing an antispasmodic.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE CG61 requires red flags to be investigated first; NICE HTG690 offers FIT for a change in bowel habit.
items.fix: Ask “is this new?” early, then explain kindly why IBS does not fit.

items.fail: Accepting the bleeding as “just from going so often”.
items.why: At 50 and over, unexplained rectal bleeding is itself an indication for FIT (NICE HTG690).
items.fix: Characterise it, then include it in your reasoning out loud: “with the blood and the weight loss, we check.”

items.fail: Telling her a negative FIT means she is in the clear.
items.why: NICE HTG690: a low FIT needs safety-netting, and referral should not be delayed if strong concern persists.
items.fix: “If the test is low but you’re still unwell, we keep going.”

items.fail: Contradicting her self-diagnosis bluntly — “it’s definitely not IBS, you shouldn’t trust the internet”.
items.why: Dismissing her research damages the relationship she needs to accept the plan.
items.fix: Credit her reading, then explain which features make you want to check first.

items.fail: Never asking what else she has wondered about.
items.why: “Does not explore the patient’s health understanding.” The colleague’s diagnosis is the hidden agenda.
items.fix: “Has anyone close to you had bowel trouble recently?”

items.fail: Offering a mid-morning appointment next week to a teacher who says she can’t get away.
items.why: A plan that does not fit her life will not happen; examiners reward tailoring.
items.fix: One early visit for FIT kit, bloods and examination.

items.fail: Closing with “we’ll be in touch with the results”.
items.why: No named triggers and no owner for the result are standard failing feedback statements.
items.fix: Name the A&E triggers, say you will ring with the FIT result, and check understanding.

timeMap.d: Identity and privacy on the phone. She offers the IBS label and the stress. Agree to understand the symptoms first.
New or lifelong? Duration, bleeding, weight, tiredness, night symptoms, pain, family history. The ‘new at 59’ answer is the pivot.
Gently invite what else she has wondered. The colleague with bowel cancer surfaces; validate the self-soothing label.
Not safely IBS. FIT (NICE NG12: at least 10 µg Hb/g → suspected cancer pathway), bloods, coeliac serology, face-to-face exam. Low FIT is not an all-clear.
A&E triggers, an early-morning visit that fits her timetable, GP owns the result, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Agrees it sounds like IBS and prescribes an antispasmodic; accepts the bleeding as “from going so often”; never asks if the change is new; no FIT, bloods or examination; never learns about the colleague.
wordPics.pass: Recognises new altered bowel habit with bleeding and weight loss at 59 as needing investigation; arranges FIT, bloods and examination; states the referral threshold; acknowledges her worry; gives a safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains kindly why IBS does not fit; surfaces the colleague’s diagnosis and names the self-soothing label without judgement; explains that a low FIT does not override persisting symptoms; fits the plan around her school day; owns the result; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “It does sound like IBS with all that stress — try mebeverine and see how you get on.”
avoid.instead: “I can’t safely call this IBS — it’s new, and there’s blood and weight loss. Let’s check properly first.”
avoid.why: Newly labelling IBS at 59 with red flags is the classic anchoring error this station tests.

avoid.dont: “If the FIT is negative, you can relax — it’s not cancer.”
avoid.instead: “If the test is low but you’re still having symptoms, we keep going — the test doesn’t overrule you.”
avoid.why: NICE HTG690 asks for safety-netting and referral when strong concern persists despite a low FIT.

avoid.dont: “You really need to stop worrying about work and put yourself first.”
avoid.instead: “Let’s fit this around your timetable — one visit before school, and a camera test is usually a single morning.”
avoid.why: Dismissing the practical barrier loses her; solving it gets the tests done.

If it comes back above a set level, national guidance says you’re referred on the urgent suspected cancer pathway, usually for a camera test. SCA_MODELS.why: FIT with the NICE NG12 threshold, bloods, coeliac serology and examination

SCA_MODELS.text: And if the test is fine?
Then we don’t just stop. If your symptoms carry on and I’m still concerned, I can refer you anyway. The test guides us — it doesn’t overrule what you’re telling me.
SCA_MODELS.why: Safety-net for a low FIT with persisting symptoms

SCA_MODELS.text: I can’t take time off mid-term, though. We’re short as it is.

I understand. Let’s make this as light-touch as possible. You could collect the FIT kit and have your bloods and examination in one visit — before school or after? If you do need a camera test, it’s usually a single morning, and your health has to come before the timetable.
SCA_MODELS.why: Problem-solves the work barrier while holding the priority

SCA_MODELS.text: I could come at eight tomorrow.
Perfect. I’ll book that. I won’t prescribe anything for IBS today — I don’t want to damp down symptoms we need to understand. We can talk about settling things once we have answers.
SCA_MODELS.why: Declines the antispasmodic and explains why

SCA_MODELS.text: If the bleeding gets heavier, you pass clots, feel faint, get severe tummy pain or can’t open your bowels at all, go to A&E. I’ll look at the FIT result myself and ring you, and if it meets the level I’ll send the referral that day.
SCA_MODELS.why: Named emergency triggers and ownership of the result

SCA_MODELS.text: Before we finish — what will you take away from this call?
That it probably isn’t IBS, and it might be nothing, but I need the stool test, bloods and an examination tomorrow, and a camera if the test is up. And A&E if it gets bad.
Exactly right. Thank you for being so open about your colleague — that took courage.

SCA_STEM.name: Diane Foster
SCA_STEM.recent: Teacher. BMI 26. No FIT, FBC or coeliac serology on record. No known family history of bowel cancer.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call requested for “something for my IBS”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE HTG690 (2023, formerly DG56) — FIT in primary care · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE CG61 (2008, updated 2017) — IBS in adults · NICE NG20 (2015) — coeliac disease
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A new change in bowel habit at 59, with rectal bleeding and weight loss, is not a safe IBS diagnosis. Offer FIT, bloods and an examination; FIT at least 10 µg Hb/g means a suspected cancer pathway referral.

points.h: IBS is not a new diagnosis at 59 with red flags
points.t: NICE CG61: consider IBS when abdominal pain or discomfort, bloating or change in bowel habit has been present for at least 6 months. It lists red flags that need investigation first, including rectal bleeding, unexplained weight loss, anaemia, a mass, and a change to looser or more frequent stools for more than 6 weeks in someone over 60. Diane’s symptoms are new, 10 weeks old, with bleeding and weight loss.

NICE HTG690: offer quantitative FIT to guide referral in adults with a change in bowel habit, or aged 50 and over with unexplained rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or weight loss. She qualifies on more than one count.

NICE NG12: refer on a suspected cancer pathway for colorectal cancer if FIT is at least 10 µg Hb/g faeces. A rectal mass, an unexplained anal mass or unexplained anal ulceration is referred without FIT.

points.h: A low FIT is not an all-clear
points.t: NICE HTG690: if FIT is below 10 µg Hb/g, safety-net, and do not delay referral to an appropriate pathway if strong clinical concern persists because of ongoing unexplained symptoms.

FBC and ferritin for iron deficiency; coeliac serology (NICE NG20: IgA tTG with total IgA as first choice) for persistent unexplained bowel symptoms; abdominal examination and DRE face to face. These run alongside FIT, never instead of it.
Blood on the paper from straining or frequency is common, but at 50 and over unexplained rectal bleeding is itself a reason for FIT. Explaining it away as ‘going so often’ is the anchoring trap.

Suspected cancer pathway referral is still often called the two-week wait. The NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (October 2023) aims for cancer to be diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral; colonoscopy is usually one morning.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Identity and privacy checked; open question; let her explain her symptoms and her own label before narrowing.
Teacher in a pressured Ofsted term, skipping meals, the difficulty of time off mid-term.
“Probably just from going so much” and “it’s stress” picked up; the colleague’s diagnosis surfaced gently.
Idea (stress-related IBS), hidden concern (bowel cancer like her colleague), expectation (confirmation of IBS and tablets).
FIT; FBC, ferritin and coeliac serology; face-to-face abdominal examination and DRE.
Colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease, haemorrhoids, IBS; new onset at 59 weighed against the IBS pattern.
Asked about onset, bleeding, weight, tiredness, night symptoms, pain, mass and family history; knows a mass means referral without FIT.
Explains clearly that this cannot safely be called IBS and needs investigation for a bowel cause, including cancer.
FIT with the NICE NG12 threshold (at least 10 µg Hb/g → suspected cancer pathway); referral still possible with a low FIT and persisting concern; no antispasmodic as a substitute.
Acknowledges work stress without letting it explain the symptoms; iron deficiency and coeliac disease looked for.
A&E triggers, dated visit, GP owns the FIT result and referral, teach-back.

social.t: A teacher in a high-stakes inspection term may minimise symptoms to avoid time off. Offer early or late appointments and plain information about how long procedures take.
A peer’s cancer diagnosis is a common hidden driver of both fear and denial. Naming it lets her engage with the plan rather than avoid it.

legal.t: She self-certifies for the first 7 days of sickness absence; a single procedure day does not need a fit note. If longer absence follows, a fit note can support adjustments or time off.
If sedation is used for colonoscopy she must not drive home and will need someone to collect her.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): arrange an in-person assessment when a telephone consultation cannot meet the patient’s needs safely — here, abdominal examination and DRE.
GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): explain why a rectal examination is needed, offer a chaperone, obtain consent and document it.
The requesting clinician is responsible for acting on the FIT result. Practice systems should track suspected cancer referrals and unreturned FIT kits.

community.t: Bowel Cancer UK and Macmillan Cancer Support for information; Coeliac UK if serology is positive; Education Support’s helpline for staff wellbeing in schools.

redFlags: New change in bowel habit at 59 — looser, more frequent, urgency — for about 10 weeks
Rectal bleeding (bright red on the paper) and unintended weight loss
Ask about tiredness, night symptoms, pain, a mass and family history
psychosocial: Teacher in a stressful Ofsted term; skipping meals
A colleague of similar age recently diagnosed with bowel cancer
ice: Idea: “It’s IBS brought on by stress”
Concern: that she has bowel cancer like her colleague
Expectation: IBS confirmed and tablets to settle it

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be honest that IBS does not fit: “IBS usually comes and goes over years and doesn’t cause bleeding or weight loss. A new change at 59 with blood and weight loss needs checking for a bowel cause, including cancer — most people turn out fine, but we check.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “IBS is like a car that has always made a certain noise. Yours has suddenly started making a new one, with a warning light on — so we look under the bonnet before deciding it’s the old noise.”

management.reflectIce: “After what happened to your colleague, it makes complete sense you reached for ‘stress’. The quickest way to stop the worry running the show is a proper answer.”
management.psychosocial: Fit the tests around her school day: one early visit for FIT kit, bloods and examination; explain that a camera test is usually a single morning.
sharedPlan: FIT; NICE NG12: at least 10 µg Hb/g → suspected cancer pathway colorectal referral
FBC, ferritin and coeliac serology (NICE NG20); abdominal examination and DRE with chaperone — refer without FIT if a mass is found
No antispasmodic today; if FIT is low but symptoms persist and concern is strong, refer anyway (NICE HTG690)
safetyNet: Heavier bleeding, clots, faintness, severe pain or unable to open bowels → A&E
GP rings with the FIT result and sends any referral that day; review if symptoms persist whatever the result

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap here is agreeing with a well-read patient. The history is quick to take; marks are lost by accepting ‘IBS and stress’, by treating a low FIT as a full stop, or by missing the colleague behind the fear.

items.fail: Agreeing it sounds like IBS and prescribing an antispasmodic.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE CG61 requires red flags to be investigated first; NICE HTG690 offers FIT for a change in bowel habit.
items.fix: Ask “is this new?” early, then explain kindly why IBS does not fit.

items.fail: Accepting the bleeding as “just from going so often”.
items.why: At 50 and over, unexplained rectal bleeding is itself an indication for FIT (NICE HTG690).
items.fix: Characterise it, then include it in your reasoning out loud: “with the blood and the weight loss, we check.”

items.fail: Telling her a negative FIT means she is in the clear.
items.why: NICE HTG690: a low FIT needs safety-netting, and referral should not be delayed if strong concern persists.
items.fix: “If the test is low but you’re still unwell, we keep going.”

items.fail: Contradicting her self-diagnosis bluntly — “it’s definitely not IBS, you shouldn’t trust the internet”.
items.why: Dismissing her research damages the relationship she needs to accept the plan.
items.fix: Credit her reading, then explain which features make you want to check first.

items.fail: Never asking what else she has wondered about.
items.why: “Does not explore the patient’s health understanding.” The colleague’s diagnosis is the hidden agenda.
items.fix: “Has anyone close to you had bowel trouble recently?”

items.fail: Offering a mid-morning appointment next week to a teacher who says she can’t get away.
items.why: A plan that does not fit her life will not happen; examiners reward tailoring.
items.fix: One early visit for FIT kit, bloods and examination.

items.fail: Closing with “we’ll be in touch with the results”.
items.why: No named triggers and no owner for the result are standard failing feedback statements.
items.fix: Name the A&E triggers, say you will ring with the FIT result, and check understanding.
